title: How science works: applications, validation and society
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: NEW-nature-of-science-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; NEW-nature-of-science-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; NEW-nature-of-science-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; NEW-nature-of-science-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: NEW-nature-of-science-1#N.3, NEW-nature-of-science-1#N.6, NEW-nature-of-science-1#N.8, NEW-nature-of-science-1#N.9.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Risk
items.clue: Depends on how likely harm is and how serious it would be.

items.label: Replication
items.clue: Other teams repeat the work, ideally with different equipment.

items.label: Peer review
items.clue: Independent experts scrutinise a paper before a journal publishes it.

items.label: Integrity
items.clue: Reporting all results honestly, stating uncertainties and declaring conflicts of interest.

questions.stem: Many home smoke alarms contain a tiny sealed source of americium-241, an alpha emitter. Which statement is the best scientific evaluation?

options.text: They should be banned, since no radioactive source in a home is ever acceptable.
The added risk is very small and unlikely; the lives saved by early warning far outweigh it.
They carry no risk at all, because alpha particles cannot pass through skin.
The decision depends only on whether radioactive alarms are cheaper than other types.

questions.explanation: Correct. Alpha particles are stopped by the casing, so harm is unlikely while the source stays sealed. The benefit, warning of fire, is large.

questions.stem: A surprising result passes peer review and is published. Two other laboratories then repeat the experiment: one gets the same result, the other does not. What should scientists conclude?

options.text: The result is established: it passed peer review and one laboratory confirmed it.
The result is disproved: one failed replication outweighs the other evidence.
It is not yet established: the cause of the disagreement must be found and tested.
Two results out of three agree, so the majority view should be accepted.

questions.explanation: Correct. Conflicting replications are checked for faults on both sides, as OPERA's timing was, until the evidence agrees.

questions.stem: A town is deciding whether to allow a new mobile-phone mast near a school. Which question can science answer directly?

options.text: Whether the town's residents should accept the mast
Whether the mast is worth the change to the view from the school
Whether better phone coverage for the town matters more than the residents' worries
Whether radio-wave exposure at the school would be below the recommended limits

questions.explanation: Correct. Exposure can be measured or calculated and compared with limits set from the evidence on harm.

questions.stem: A company's paper on a battery that fully charges in one minute passes peer review. Independent laboratories ask for samples to test, but the company refuses. What is the best judgement about the claim?

options.text: Accept it: peer review has already confirmed that the battery works.
Treat it as unconfirmed: it is not established until others can test it.
Reject it as false: refusing to share samples proves that the battery fails.
Accept it: the company's own repeated tests all gave the same result.

questions.explanation: Correct. Validation needs independent replication by people with no stake in the result.
